title: What the Stone Still Asks
logline: An eight-metre slab of granite cut to the shape of a palm-leaf book lies on its back among the ruined shrines of a medieval capital, and one sentence on it asks its readers to unite and remove a man who has done nothing but think of something. What he was to have thought has worn off the stone. The urging has not.
human_question: When a sentence asks me to push someone away for what they might be thinking, whose mind is that, the writer's or mine if I agree?

place.what_kind_of_place: A walled terrace of stone shrines at the heart of a ruined twelfth-century royal city in the dry zone: a circular relic shrine ringed with carved stone screens, a gutted two-storey relic house, a stepped brick tower, colonnades of bare pillars. Along the east side of the relic house, raised on a low bed of short stone pillars laid crosswise, lies one enormous oblong slab, its ends pointing north and south. Its top was dressed flat and divided by narrow raised ridges into three leaves, copying the bare strips and string-holes of a palm-leaf manuscript, and every leaf is incised edge to edge with small letters between ruled lines. A double file of carved geese runs round all four sides, and at each end a goddess sits between two elephants pouring water over her. It is the longest inscription in the island, and it can be read like a page, lying down.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Two scales in one frame. The terrace is one of the finest groups of ruins in the island, pale stone and dark brick under big dry-zone trees, with a circular shrine whose screens throw rings of shadow in low sun. And the slab, which in flat light reads as a grey block, changes completely when the sun is low and raking: four thousand three hundred letters stand up in relief as rows of tiny shadows, the leaf-ridges become lines of light, and the geese round the rim turn into a frieze of small round bodies. The film's move is a reading: a camera travelling sideways and level across the page at the speed of an eye, which, without a cut and without climbing, runs off the end of the stone and on across the terrace into the buildings the stone claims.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Only the light, and the camera. The raking window lasts about forty minutes after the sun clears the trees; after that the letters flatten and the stone goes back to grey. The worn third leaf, where the letters grow shallow and in places vanish, is the one part of the surface that stays blank however the light falls. Birds and wind; no people, because the film is shot in the first light before the site fills.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry season, on a clear morning, in the first direct sun from the east, low enough to rake across the lines of letters. Flat overcast light or high sun makes the inscription nearly invisible, and the whole film depends on the raking window.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A morning film in a ruined royal city. First the terrace wide and empty in blue shade; then the sun reaching one long grey stone and the letters on it rising out of the surface as shadows; the carved geese round its rim; the goddess and her two elephants at its end. Then one continuous sideways move, low and level, across the lettered surface, over a stretch where the letters have worn to nothing, off the end of the stone and on across the paving until the carved screens of the circular shrine fill the frame in full sun. A viewer with no interest in philosophy gets a complete piece: dark to light, a hidden text surfacing, a single unbroken move with a destination.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same move becomes a reading of one sentence. The stone tells a summoned subject he may come without fear if he has done no wrong, then, a few lines on, asks the people to shun and remove any man of a named class of the king's subjects who so much as thinks of something, and it is exactly the something that has worn away. The voice sets that sentence beside the texts: two minds rooted in hate that differ only in whether the harm comes unbidden or at another's urging; a list of occasions that includes 'when one thinks others will do wrong'; ill will, the wish that another be destroyed, fixed in both; and a ranking by birth that the texts put in a different mind altogether. It never says what the king felt. The stone cannot show a mind; it can only show what it asks, and the only mind it asks for is the reader's. This is the one film in its group whose camera never climbs: it reads at the height of the page and keeps that height when the page runs out.

sequence.on_screen: Before sunrise, then the first minutes of direct sun. Ground level, wide, locked: an empty terrace of ruins, the circular shrine and its screens, the gutted relic house, the stepped tower, big trees. At the edge of the frame, raised on low stone blocks, a long grey slab. The sun reaches it and nothing else yet.
sequence.voice: Near the end of the twelfth century a king named Nissanka Malla had one stone brought to this terrace, to be written on. It was cut to the shape of a palm-leaf book, more than eight metres long, and its editor called it by far the longest inscription known in the island: seventy-two lines, more than four thousand three hundred letters, lying on their back and facing the sky.

sequence.on_screen: Close, in raking light: the incised lines standing up as rows of small shadows; the narrow ridges dividing the page into three leaves, copied from a palm-leaf manuscript; along the rim, the double file of carved geese; at the south end, the goddess seated between two elephants pouring water.
sequence.voice: Most of it is praise: the king's birth, his gifts, his buildings, set down at his own court. The scholar who edited it a century ago, Wickremasinghe, said its purpose was political, and he went on to guess at what the king must have felt. This film does not guess. A stone has no mind, and there is no face left here to read. What it has is sentences.

sequence.on_screen: The camera lifts just clear of the stone and begins to travel sideways along the third leaf, level, a metre or two above the letters, at the pace of an eye reading a line.
sequence.voice: Near the end, the stone turns to advice for the people. A subject summoned before the king, it says, should be able to go without fear, saying: seeing I have done no wrong, what does it matter to me? The texts this series follows count fear as a form of aversion, the mind judging a thing too strong for it and wanting to get away. The fear they praise is another word altogether, the dread of doing wrong. This line holds out freedom from the first to a subject who can say he has done no wrong.

sequence.on_screen: The same move continues. The letters grow shallower; for a stretch the surface is worn smooth and blank; then letters again.
sequence.voice: A few lines further on, the stone moves from deeds to thoughts. If any man of a named class of the king's own subjects, whatever titles he already holds, were to think of, and here the letters are worn away, the people should not associate with him. He would be an object of scorn, like crows and jackals trying to copy the bearing of swans and lions. Therefore, it says, the people should unite and remove him.

sequence.on_screen: Down at the rim, very low: the carved geese in single file, one after another across the whole frame, each small body picked out by the low sun.
sequence.voice: The same bird as that sentence's swans runs round the edge of the stone, carved as ornament: the kind the crow may not copy. The sentence measures people by birth, and then it asks for a removal. The texts keep those two apart. Holding oneself high by birth and lineage over those counted low is a form of conceit, and conceit belongs only with minds rooted in greed; the pushing-away that wants a thing gone belongs only with the two minds rooted in hate. So no single moment of mind could agree with the whole sentence. A reader who did would need at least two, one after the other. A few lines earlier the same stone had told its readers not to become proud.

sequence.on_screen: Back on the traverse, level and unhurried, as the sharp letters return and the far end of the slab comes towards the lens.
sequence.voice: The texts name two minds rooted in hate, alike in everything but one: whether the harm comes of one's own accord, or after someone else's urging. The wish that another be destroyed is fixed in both. And among the occasions for them they list the quietest there is: when one thinks that others will do wrong. This sentence asks for a removal over a thought, before any deed. It is an urging, addressed to whoever reads it. Whose mind wrote it cannot be seen. The mind it asks for is the reader's. Whether a stone can urge at all, the texts do not say.

sequence.on_screen: Still without a cut and still at the same height, the move runs off the end of the stone and carries on across the paving, past the relic house and towards the circular shrine, the sun now full on its carved screens.
sequence.voice: Almost nothing about this stone is as settled as it looks. A second slab of the same king, at a gate of the same city, says outright what the worn words most likely said: the throne. The stone claims these buildings for him; the archaeologist who first surveyed them thought some of the king's buildings were really an earlier king's. Even where the stone was quarried turns on one vowel sign, a sacred hill or a rock fortress, and the vowel may have been scratched out.

sequence.on_screen: The move slows and stops against the carved screens of the circular shrine in full morning sun, held. No voice for most of the hold.
sequence.voice: What the man was to have thought has worn off the stone. The urging to remove him has not worn at all. Eight hundred years of readers have walked past it, and the stone is still asking the same thing of each of them.

concept_merge.why_together: C007 supplies the two hate-rooted minds and their one difference, whether the harm is done on one's own wish or after someone's urging [C007-M:L9; C007-P:L25–L28], with ill will, the wish that others be destroyed, fixed in both [C007-P:L53], and a list of occasions that includes 'when one thinks others will do wrong' [C007-M:L17]. C022 supplies what the stone's own simile does: it measures by birth, which Pradeepika names as birth-conceit [C022-P:L107] and places only in greed-rooted minds [C022-P:L101], while hate as a factor occurs only in the two hate-rooted minds [C022-P:L121]. It also supplies the two fears the stone's advice to summoned subjects stands between: fear as aversion that judges its object too strong and means to get away [C022-P:L121], and the dread of wrongdoing whose absence is a fault [C022-P:L63]. Put on one sentence, the two digests do something neither does alone: C007 says what kind of mind such a sentence asks for, and C022 says that the ranking and the removal cannot be one mind at all.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That a written urging is a strange object for this doctrine. The sources classify minds, not stones; they never say whether a text can prompt, and they give 'by one's own hand or through others' as part of the unprompted mind's example [C007-P:L59], so an order passed to others is not automatically the prompted mind. The film therefore refuses the easy move of reading the king's mind off his stone, and places the only mind it can honestly locate where the stone itself places it: in the reader it addresses. The pairing also exposes the sentence's structure without a verdict on anyone. The C022 finding that conceit and hate never share a moment turns one line into at least two minds in sequence, the measuring and the pushing-away, and the stone's own earlier warning against pride sits a few lines above the ranking. The worn lacuna, which removes exactly what the man was to have thought, leaves the urging standing without its object, which is the digest's quietest occasion, suspicion of a wrong not yet done, made visible as blank stone.

concept_links.why: C007 needs a hate-rooted act that is visibly asked for rather than done, because the two hate-rooted minds differ only in whether the harm is done on one's own wish with nobody's urging or 'with urging' [C007-M:L9], a split Pradeepika gives the same way, the second mind being like the first except for the urging, support and encouragement behind it [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-P:L38; C007-P:L63]. The slab's removal clause is an urging in the imperative, addressed to the public; its target has done nothing but think, which is Margaya's occasion 'when one thinks others will do wrong' [C007-M:L17]; and what it asks for, that the man 'be wiped out with his worldly possessions' and that the people 'unite and remove him', is the wish that another be destroyed, which Pradeepika says is fixed in these minds [C007-P:L53], the aversion that wants its object destroyed [C007-P:L32–L34]. Two digest cautions shape the film. First, Pradeepika's own example of killing 'by one's own hand or through others' sits under the unprompted mind [C007-P:L59], so the film never equates an order with the prompted mind and never names the writer's mind; it places the prompt on the reader and says the texts do not decide whether a stone can urge. Second, the sources make no exception for anger that feels justified [C007-M:L11], while the stone presents its maxims as compassion and a king's punishments as a physician's remedy; the film neither adopts the stone's account of itself nor calls it hate. The does_not_transfer line on bodily effects [C007-P:L47] is kept: nothing is said about what such a mind does to a body.

Three C022 findings land on the same stone. Fear is the aversion that judges its object strong and means to get away from it [C022-P:L121], and the dread of wrongdoing is a different factor, praised through the fault of its absence [C022-P:L63]; the stone's line that a summoned subject may come 'without fear' because 'I have done no wrong' stands between them, and the digest's own warning that 'fear is healthy survival instinct' does not map onto the source keeps the film from calling that fearlessness healthy or the summons hateful. Birth-conceit, 'I descend from a high birth-lineage', is a form of conceit [C022-P:L107; C022-P:L103–L111], and conceit is found only in greed-rooted minds [C022-P:L101], while hate occurs only in the two hate-rooted minds [C022-P:L121]; the sentence that ranks crows against swans and then orders a removal therefore cannot, on the texts' account, be a single mind. The digest's other limit is load-bearing here: Pradeepika's conceit is about how a person measures himself, not a teaching against or for social equality [C022-P:L109], so the film never turns it into a verdict on caste, on equality, or on the class the stone names, and never names that class in the voice.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a sentence can carry an urging long after anyone can say what mind wrote it; that the texts' two hate-rooted minds differ only in whether the harm is asked for; that one of the occasions they list is simply suspecting a wrong that has not been done; and that a line which ranks people by birth and then asks for their removal is, on the texts' own account, at least two different minds in succession. The proof is physical: the worn blank where the man's thought should be, and the unworn words asking for his removal.
what_must_be_real: The stone, the raking light and the worn stretch as they are. No letters are restored, graded in, composited or projected; the lacuna is never filled on screen, and no caption translates the missing words. The traverse is one real unbroken move or, if that cannot be permitted, it is honestly cut, never stitched to look continuous. No visitor, guard, sweeper or devotee is framed; the terrace is filmed empty in the first light. The class the stone names, and the dynasties it tells people never to establish, are not named on screen or in the voice. No mind is attributed to the king, to the stone's composers or to anyone the stone mentions; the voice quotes the stone and its editor as texts. Nothing about the king's alleged campaigns, his accession or his death enters the film.
position_hint: Early in the anger-and-fear stage: the film that introduces the two hate-rooted minds and the prompted one, before the films that turn to fear as retreat, to suspicion, and to remorse. It asks the viewer the group's question at its quietest, about a sentence rather than a blow.
risks: Reading the king's mind off his stone. The editor's own introduction guesses at what the king 'must have felt'; the film mentions that there was a guess and declines to repeat it. No person, historical or present, is narrated or framed as angry, afraid, envious or proud.

Taking half of a passage. The same stone says its king burned with indignation and that the gifts of a neighbouring royal house quenched the flame, and that another king and his mother were filled with fear; both lines belong to its account of an overseas campaign, which is war and which its own editor said 'must not be taken as literally true'. Taking the images without the campaign would be telling the passage halfway; taking the campaign would break the floor. None of it is used.

Entering a live identity dispute. The stone names a caste of the king's own subjects and tells people never to establish non-Buddhist kings of named neighbouring dynasties. Both lines have modern political uses. The voice says only 'a named class of the king's own subjects', and never quotes the dynasty line at all.

Turning the conceit doctrine into a teaching about caste or social equality. The C022 digest forbids exactly this reading of its conceit passage; the film applies the doctrine to the sentence's simile only, and says nothing about whether any class of people is higher, lower or equal.

Treating the stone as hate. The C007 digest makes no exception for justified anger, but the film is not allowed to convert that into a verdict either; the stone calls its advice compassion, and the film neither accepts nor refutes that. It asks what mind the sentence asks for, and leaves the writer's unread.

Equating an order with the prompted mind. Pradeepika's 'through others' example sits under the unprompted mind. The film places the prompt on the reader, and says the texts do not decide whether a written urging counts.

The threshold-stone failure. An inscription lying on the ground is exactly what the standing decisions call true and unwatchable. The film survives it only if the raking light is caught and the traverse carries into the terrace; without both it is a flat grey block.

Overlap within the group. The group's film with a king's own written justification (a shore, in wind, IDEA-0035) sits nearby. This film is kept apart by kind (a lying text), time (first direct sun), movement (one level traverse at page height) and by quoting no chronicle.

A second film by the same king's stone-cutters: a GRP-04 film at a citadel carries one of his slabs and ends on a vertical aerial climb. This film therefore never climbs, and never names the citadel's story.

Archetype collision found in audit: IDEA-0025 (GRP-02) opens and closes on an inscribed stone and moves a lens across its carved lines. Inscription-led films are one archetype under the method; this film is the purer case, but the two now share both the kind of object and the reading move, and the reviewer should choose or one should be reframed.
drop_if: No low traverse can be permitted over the slab (drone, cable-cam or overhead slider) and no honest ground alternative carries the reading move; a cut version is acceptable only if it still ends on the terrace in full sun.
The raking light cannot be caught because the slab is now shaded, roofed or fenced in a way that blocks the low eastern sun.
A recce with Wickremasinghe's plates cannot locate the worn stretch of the removal sentence on the surface; the payoff then has no object and the film is re-planned or dropped.
Filming at first light inside the terrace is refused, so that the only possible footage is of a crowded site at midday.

connections.note: The same king's stone-cutters at two sites. There, a citadel whose slab of his records the palace in good order, in a film about precautions that could not prevent what they were meant to prevent, ending on a vertical climb. Here, the longest of his texts, in which a precaution is written as an urging to remove a man for a thought. This film never climbs and does not tell the citadel's story.

The same ruined city seen from its reservoir: a high, wide water film at first light and last light about a chronicle's count. This film stays at page height inside the terrace at the city's centre and uses no chronicle.

The same group's film on a king's order and his own written justification on a shore, the group's film on anger that claims to be just. Both rest on words a king had written down; this one never judges the writer and turns the question onto the reader, while that one holds its king's claim of justice against the sources' refusal of any exception.

A GRP-02 film on a seafront lawn that opens and closes on an inscribed stone post stating what its walk was for, filmed with a lens moving across the carved lines. The method treats inscription-led films as one archetype and this film is wholly one; that film's spine is a lawn and a crowd, but its argument also rests on a cut text read by a moving lens. Flagged in audit, not resolved.

selection.reason: Carries C007's prompted hate-rooted mind on a documented, primary text that asks exactly that question: an urging, in the imperative, to remove a man for a thought, on a colossal worked stone in one of the island's great ruin groups. The C022 findings on fear, birth-conceit and the separation of greed-side and hate-side factors all land on the same stone without adjustment of the concepts. The location was chosen blind as a proposal and re-verified here against the primary edition; several of its popular facts were corrected.

review.note:
The body of this record was replaced entirely on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-03 rework and rebuilt from fresh research; the previous body was not read. Under standing decision 9 the verdict is pending; the old status was also pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset. The concepts are unchanged (C007 primary, C022 supporting). The location, named in suggested_location, is a twelfth-century royal slab-inscription lying in the central terrace of a ruined capital; it takes its district from 3 to 4 films among those currently written, as set out in the research note. It was a blind colleague's proposal and was tested, not assumed: both halves of the method hold (a primary text that turns on the prompted hate-rooted mind and on suspicion of a wrong not yet done; a first-rate ruin group with a colossal worked stone in it), but the proposal's treatment (a top-down drone rising vertically) was replaced because a GRP-04 film at another of the same king's inscription sites already pays off on a vertical climb. The new treatment is a single level traverse at page height in the first raking sun, across the worn removal sentence and on into the terrace, with no climb. Corrections made to the proposal and to popular sources: the earliest translation is Armour's in the Ceylon Almanac of 1834, not Müller's of 1883; Müller did not read a different name on the stone but argued that the engraver altered one vowel on purpose to name a more sacred hill, and Wickremasinghe, seeing possible erasure of an i-vowel, allowed he 'may be right'; the inscription does not say the relic house beside it was built in sixty hours, although Wikipedia says it does; the '25 tonnes' figure is unsourced and its most-copied form ('25 tonnes (5,512 lbs)') contradicts itself, while Bell's measurements imply something between about 13 and 20 tonnes if the stone is granite (this record's arithmetic, not a published figure); a Commons caption's breadth of 4.25 m is wrong (Bell: 4 ft 7 in); the removal sentence's gap is real and its fill ('kingship') comes from a separate slab of the same king (EZ II no. 28), not from this one. The strongest objection is the threshold-stone rule: a text lying on the ground. The answer offered is that this stone is itself a colossal carved object and that the traverse carries the reading into the terrace the stone claims; if the raking light or the low move cannot be had, the film should be dropped, not weakened. Still unverified: everything on the ground, including where on the surface the worn stretch lies, current opening hours, and whether any low traverse would be permitted in the sacred terrace.

Audit 2026-09-26: independent second check against Wickremasinghe, EZ II no. 17 (pp. 98-123, read in the scratch OCR and the SIDDHAM translation), no. 28 and no. 29, and against the C007 and C022 source lines. The removal sentence, the 'without fear' advice, the pride warning, the crow-and-swan simile, the 211 hamsas, Bell's measurements, Müller's Sagiri argument and Wickremasinghe's 'may be right', the 'special purpose' and 'must have felt' passages all read as quoted; the simile likens the aspirant to crows aping swans, and 'unite and remove him' is Wickremasinghe's wording. The doctrine checks: C007-M:L17 does list 'when one thinks others will do wrong', C007-P:L53 fixes ill will, C022-P:L101 puts conceit only in greed-rooted minds and C022-P:L121 hate only in the two hate-rooted ones, and C022-P:L107 covers both 'I descend from a high lineage' and the high-born's conceit towards those counted low. Changed: (1) beat 5 said the sentence 'is at least two [minds]', which reads the writer's mind and breaks the film's own rule and the floor on identifiable persons; it now puts the two minds on a reader who agreed with the sentence. The same beat said the rim geese 'are the birds of that sentence'; they are ornament, so the voice now says only that the same bird runs round the stone. (2) Beat 1's 'brought a very long way' took one side of the Mihintale/Sigiri dispute (Müller put Sigiri 'only about 15 miles' off); removed. 'Still the longest inscription in the island' is now the editor's 'by far the longest known'. (3) Beat 7 said the first surveyors thought some buildings were 'begun by' an earlier king; EZ II no. 29 reports Bell's opinion that several buildings credited to Nissanka Malla were Parakramabahu I's; reworded, singular. (4) Beat 3's 'promises' became 'holds out' (the stone advises). (5) Connection and risk referring to IDEA-0045's old proposal removed; IDEA-0035 is now written, so its connection is no longer 'proposed'; the research note's group comparison and district count no longer rely on reopened slots. (6) A collision found in audit is recorded: IDEA-0025 is also built on an inscribed stone read by a moving lens. Images: the two Gal Pota files were confirmed through the Commons API. Still unverified: where the worn stretch lies on the surface, the light angle, any traverse permission. The strongest objection is still the threshold-stone rule, now with a second inscription film on the rework slate.

suggested_location.name: The Galpota ('stone book') slab-inscription of Nissanka Malla, beside the Hatadage in the Dalada Maluwa (the Quadrangle), ancient city of Polonnaruwa
suggested_location.region: Polonnaruwa District, North Central Province: inside the Dalada Maluwa (the Quadrangle) of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa, on the east side of the Hatadage and a few metres south-west of the Satmahal Prasada, within the UNESCO World Heritage property of the Ancient City of Polonnaruwa
suggested_location.why_here: Because the text and the object ask C007's question in the same place. Nissanka Malla's Galpota is the only surviving document found here that puts an urging in the imperative to a public ('the people should unite and remove him') against a man who has only thought of something, and whose own surface has since worn away exactly the something he was to have thought, while leaving the urging whole. C007 turns on whether a hate-rooted act comes on one's own wish or at another's urging, and lists suspicion of a wrong not yet done among its occasions; C022 turns on fear, on birth-conceit and on the rule that greed-side and hate-side factors never share a moment, and the stone's advice to summoned subjects, its crow-and-swan simile and its removal order sit within a few lines of each other. And the object is worth travelling for: a single slab of granite more than eight metres long, cut to the form of a palm-leaf book, framed by 211 carved geese and two Gaja-Lakshmi panels, lying in one of the island's great ruin groups, whose buildings the stone itself claims. The stone even carries the simile's swans round its own edge.

historical_thread.story:
The Galpota lies close to the eastern outer wall of the Hatadage, within a few yards south-west of the Satmahal Prasada, with its ends pointing north and south. H. C. P. Bell's measurements, quoted in Epigraphia Zeylanica II, give it as 26 ft 10 in long down its axis (26 ft 7 in at both edges), 4 ft 7 in broad, and from 2 ft 2 in to 1 ft 4 in deep. Its upper surface was smoothed, framed and divided into three partitions by narrow fillets 'in imitation of the bare spaces on the palm leaves of ola manuscripts', and the record, 'seventy-two lines, containing more than 4,300 letters', was incised between ruled lines in letters about 1¼ in high; it is 'by far the longest known in Ceylon'. Bell recorded it raised on a brick podium under a canopy on ten pillars, resting on a 'corduroy' of short pillars laid crosswise; its sides and ends carry double bands of hamsas, which Wickremasinghe's note counts at 211, and each end a seated Lakshmi with two elephants pouring water. The third partition is worn, 'so worn off as to render it impossible in some places to make out the words'.

The text is Nissanka Malla's (reigned 1187–1196). Section A gives his descent from the Kalinga line and Vijaya, his birth in Simhapura 'when one thousand seven hundred years had elapsed' since Vijaya's arrival, his portents (clouds dispersed by a frown, a serpent that stung itself on his word), his tax remissions, gifts, and repairs to tanks; it says that 'thinking that robbers commit robbery on account of their desire for wealth, he gave them whatever things they liked and in this way he removed the fear of thieves'. Section B gives his marriages, his tulabhara gifts, his tours, and an account of an expedition to India. Section C lists his buildings in the capital, among them the Dalada-geya and the Vata-geya, and then, 'out of compassion', a set of maxims for the people. Kings are 'human divinities'; an impartial king's appearance is like a Buddha's; kings' punishments are like a physician's remedy. 'A subject should [so conduct] himself that when he is told that he has been summoned [to the presence of the king], he might go without fear, saying, "Seeing I have done no wrong, what does it matter to me?"' 'Kings do not like those who are puffed up with pride. So when one has received titles, offices, and wealth from them, he should not become proud.' Then: 'If any one ..... belonging to the Govi caste, regardless of the titles and offices he has already received, were to think of . . . . . . . . the people should not associate themselves with him. Were he to entertain such an idea, he would be held by the public as an object of scorn — as crows, jackals, &c., that try to emulate the mien of swans, lions, and the like — and he himself would be wiped out with his worldly possessions. Therefore the people should unite and remove him ......' The section goes on to the succession (princes even if minors; failing them queens; failing them 'even a slipper worn on the feet of a great king') and to the injunction not to establish 'non-buddhistic kings of Cola, Pandya [countries], &c.'. A postscript on the southern end says the stone was brought from 'Sagiri' by the Nissanka warriors under an official, Tota-danavu Mand-navan.

Who wrote it down, and what did they stand to gain. The earliest attestation is the stone itself, undated but placed by Wickremasinghe near the close of the nine-year reign, and composed at the court of the king it praises; Wickremasinghe elsewhere speaks of 'the composers of his inscriptions'. It was first translated by Armour in an appendix to Turnour's Epitome, published in the Ceylon Almanac for 1834; Müller printed a transcript and translation as no. 148 of Ancient Inscriptions of Ceylon (1883); Wickremasinghe re-edited it independently from two estampages as no. 17 in Epigraphia Zeylanica II (issued in parts, 1912–27), pp. 98–123. Bell called it 'a blatant panegyric on the greatness of Nissanka-Malla's mighty acts and munificence as assessed by himself'. Wickremasinghe agreed that it served 'a special purpose': at the king's accession Kalinga, Govi-kula, Pandya and probably Cola parties were 'perpetually intriguing for political supremacy', and the stone's policy of conciliation was undercut by 'his open antagonism to the aspirations of the nobles of the Govi-kula', whose leader had been Parakramabahu I. A second slab of the same king at the North Gate of the city (EZ II no. 28) says explicitly what the Galpota's worn line most likely said: 'People of the Govi caste should never aspire to the dignity of kingship', with a longer string of similes (the crow aping the swan, the donkey the Sindh horse, the worm the cobra-king, the firefly the sun, the jackal the lion), and threatens that those who join them 'will be rooted out'. Of the stone's claims in general, Wickremasinghe wrote that the Indian campaign 'must not be taken as literally true', that the composers may have 'credited him with the victories gained by Parakrama-Bahu I', and that 'that this is true in the case of several buildings is the opinion of Mr. Bell' (EZ II no. 29, p. 167).

The stone's origin is itself disputed. Wickremasinghe glosses 'Sagiri' as Mihintale, which fits the local tradition, recorded by Tennent, Pridham and Forbes, of a stone dragged from there; Forbes marvelled that it was moved 'upwards of eighty miles'. Müller argued that it really came from Sigiri, some fifteen miles away, and that the engraver had written Sa-giri for Si-giri to give it a more sacred character. Wickremasinghe found this unconvincing on distance, and yet allowed that 'Dr. Muller may be right', because on the estampages he seemed to see marks where an i-vowel sign above the s had been erased, and because another slab of the same king records being brought from Eraeru-galla, near Sigiri. Bell thought the Mihintale journey the likelier and put it down to 'the egregious vanity of that self-lauding monarch'. Wickremasinghe also corrected Müller's rendering 'this engraved stone', which implied the slab had been inscribed before it travelled; he read it as a blank brought for the purpose.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C007's defining split is not anger against calm but unbidden against urged: the two hate-rooted minds are alike except that the second arises with urging, support and encouragement. Most places that carry anger carry an act. This stone carries an urging, in the imperative, addressed to a public that did not yet exist when it was cut and still reads it, and it names its occasion with a precision the Margaya list would recognise: a man 'were to think of' something. That is the digest's quietest occasion, suspicion of a wrong not yet done, and the stone does not even preserve what the wrong was; the words have worn off, and what remains is the order to shun him and 'unite and remove him', the wish that another be destroyed which Pradeepika says is fixed in both hate-rooted minds. The history sharpens rather than softens this. The stone's editor said openly that the text had a political purpose and guessed at the king's feelings; the film cannot follow him there, because a camera cannot read a mind eight centuries gone and the texts classify minds, not inscriptions. What it can do is exactly what the digest's own caution demands: Pradeepika puts acting 'through others' inside the unprompted mind's example, so an order does not make its writer's mind the prompted one, and the only mind the stone can be said to prompt is the reader it addresses. C022 then divides the sentence. Its crow-and-swan simile is a measuring by birth and lineage, which the texts file as conceit and place only with greed; its removal is aversion, which they place only with hate; and they say the two kinds never share a moment. So the line cannot be one mind. The stone even preaches against pride a few lines before it ranks. And its advice that a summoned subject may come 'without fear' because he has done no wrong sits between C022's two fears, the recoil from a thing judged too strong and the dread of doing wrong, a few lines before a man who has done nothing is to be removed for a thought. None of this is analogy: it is what the text says, and the film's job is to read it at the height of the page and leave the writer's mind unread.
what_is_certain: The Galpota is a single oblong slab lying close to the eastern outer wall of the Hatadage in the Dalada Maluwa of Polonnaruwa, a few yards south-west of the Satmahal Prasada, ends pointing north and south (Wickremasinghe, EZ II no. 17, p. 98).

Bell's measurements (A.S.C. Annual Report 1903, p. 17, quoted in EZ II p. 98): 26 ft 10 in long down its axis, 26 ft 7 in at both edges; 4 ft 7 in broad; 2 ft 2 in to 1 ft 4 in deep. Bell also recorded a brick podium of about 31 ft 3 in by 13 ft 6 in and a canopy on ten pillars 5 ft high.

The upper surface is divided into three partitions (9 ft, 8 ft 7 in, 8 ft 8 in) by narrow fillets in imitation of the bare spaces of palm-leaf manuscripts; the record has seventy-two lines and more than 4,300 letters about 1¼ in high, and Wickremasinghe calls it 'by far the longest known in Ceylon' (EZ II pp. 98–99).

Its sides and ends carry double bands of hamsas (geese or swans), counted in Wickremasinghe's note at 211, and each end a seated Lakshmi with two elephants pouring water (EZ II p. 99). The third partition is badly worn, so that in places the words cannot be made out.

The text is Nissanka Malla's (1187–1196). It is undated; Wickremasinghe places it near the close of the reign. The translation quoted in this record is Wickremasinghe's (EZ II pp. 115–123), as also transcribed in the SIDDHAM database record IN03081.

Section C contains, in this order: the advice that a summoned subject should go 'without fear, saying, "Seeing I have done no wrong, what does it matter to me?"'; 'Kings do not like those who are puffed up with pride ... he should not become proud'; and the removal clause: 'If any one ..... belonging to the Govi caste ... were to think of . . . . . . . . the people should not associate themselves with him ... as crows, jackals, &c., that try to emulate the mien of swans, lions, and the like — and he himself would be wiped out with his worldly possessions. Therefore the people should unite and remove him'. The object of 'think of' is lost in a lacuna.

The same section presents the maxims as proclaimed 'out of compassion', says kings' punishments are given 'with good intentions, just as a physician applies a remedy', and tells people not to establish non-Buddhist kings of named neighbouring dynasties. The film uses none of the last.
The postscript says the stone was brought from 'Sagiri' by the Nissanka warriors under Tota-danavu Mand-navan (EZ II p. 123).

The inscription was first translated by Armour in an appendix to Turnour's Epitome of the History of Ceylon, published in the Ceylon Almanac for 1834; Müller printed it as no. 148 in Ancient Inscriptions of Ceylon (1883); Wickremasinghe's edition is EZ II no. 17 (EZ II p. 104).
The North Gate slab of the same king (EZ II no. 28) states: 'People of the Govi caste should never aspire to the dignity of kingship', with the crow and swan among a string of similes.

Wickremasinghe wrote that the Galpota was 'intended ... to serve a special purpose' amid court factions, and that its policy of conciliation was undercut by the king's 'open antagonism to the aspirations of the nobles of the Govi-kula' (EZ II pp. 101–102); and, of the king's inscriptions generally, that the Indian campaign 'must not be taken as literally true' and that, in Bell's opinion, several buildings were credited to him that belonged to Parakramabahu I (EZ II no. 29, p. 167).
what_is_disputed: Where the stone came from. Wickremasinghe glosses 'Sagiri' as Mihintale, in line with a local tradition recorded by Tennent, Pridham and Forbes; Müller (AIC p. 66) argued it came from Sigiri and that the engraver deliberately wrote Sa-giri for Si-giri; Wickremasinghe, noting possible erasure of an i-vowel sign on the estampages and a second slab of the king brought from near Sigiri, allowed that 'Dr. Muller may be right'. Both positions are kept. The widely repeated 'dragged from Mihintale' and '100 km' are one reading, not a fact. Note also a correction: Müller did not read 'Sigiri' on the stone; he read Sagiri and argued it meant Sigiri.

The weight. The widely repeated '25 tonnes' has no source found here, and its most-copied form, in a Commons/Flickr caption, reads '25 tonnes (5,512 lbs)', which contradicts itself (25 tonnes is about 55,000 lb). From Bell's dimensions, a granite slab of that size would weigh roughly 13 to 20 tonnes depending on how the depth varies; that is this record's arithmetic, not a published figure, and the film gives no weight.

What the worn line said. The Galpota's lacuna is not filled in Wickremasinghe's translation. The North Gate slab's explicit ban on the Govi caste aspiring to kingship makes 'the throne' or 'kingship' the most likely fill, and the voice says 'most likely'; it is an inference from a second text, not a reading of this one.

Which buildings are really his. The stone claims the Dalada-geya and the Vata-geya among others; Wickremasinghe identifies the Vata-geya 'most probably' with the circular relic-house (the Vatadage), and reports Bell's opinion that several buildings were credited to Nissanka Malla that belonged to Parakramabahu I. Which ones, and how far, is not settled here.

The Hatadage 'built in sixty hours'. Wikipedia's Hatadage article says the Rajavaliya, the Pujavaliya 'and the Galpotha inscription itself' say so. The Galpota does not: its Section C says only that he 'built of stone' the Dalada-geya, the Vata-geya and the flower-trail hall. The Pujavaliya and Rajavaliya passages were not reached, so the claim is held as unverified and is not used.

Whose words these are. The stone speaks in the king's name, but Wickremasinghe elsewhere refers to 'the composers of his inscriptions' and to 'the usually bombastic style of the composer of Nissanka-Malla's records'. How far the king wrote or dictated any of it is not known.

What the king felt. Wickremasinghe wrote that Nissanka Malla 'must have felt the insecurity of his regal power', and Bell spoke of his 'egregious vanity'; both are modern characterisations of a mind. This record reports that they were made and the film does not repeat them.

Small popular errors, corrected: Wikipedia's Nissanka Malla article calls the Galpota a 'rock inscription' (it is a slab brought to the site); a Commons caption gives the slab as '8 m x 4,25 m' (Bell's breadth is 4 ft 7 in, about 1.4 m).

what_to_film: The terrace wide and empty in blue shade before sunrise, locked, from ground level, with the slab at the edge of the frame; then the first direct sun reaching the slab.
The lettered surface in raking light, close and at several distances, so the shadows of the letters and the ridges between the three leaves read clearly.
The double file of carved geese along the rim, very low, in single-file compositions that fill the frame edge to edge.
The Gaja-Lakshmi panel at each end, and the postscript on the southern end face.
The worn stretch of the third leaf, located on a recce against Wickremasinghe's plates (EZ II plates 18–19 and the estampages), where the removal sentence's letters have gone.

The payoff: one continuous sideways traverse at page height, a metre or two above the stone, at reading pace along the third leaf, across the worn stretch, off the end of the slab and on across the paving at the same height to the carved screens of the Vatadage in full sun. No climb at any point.
The Hatadage's east wall and the Satmahal Prasada only as they pass through the traverse, never as separate reveals.
suggested_location.access: The Galpota lies inside the Dalada Maluwa of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa, a ticketed Central Cultural Fund site within a UNESCO World Heritage property; it is roped off from a path that runs along it. Filming inside the terrace at first light, before public opening, needs a permit from the Central Cultural Fund and the Department of Archaeology. The traverse needs either a drone flight (Civil Aviation Authority permission, Ministry of Defence clearance, and the site's own consent, which may well be refused over a sacred terrace), a cable-cam, or an overhead slider; if none is allowed, the payoff becomes a cut. The terrace is a sacred area where visitors customarily remove shoes and hats; the crew does the same. Opening hours, permit fees and current drone policy are unverified.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry season, roughly February to September, on a clear morning; the north-east monsoon rains fall mainly from October to January. The shoot needs the first forty minutes or so of direct sun from the east, before the site opens and before the light flattens the letters. The exact sun angle across the lines of letters must be checked on a recce.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 26 September 2026, done blind to this record's previous body. The primary text was read in Wickremasinghe's edition, Epigraphia Zeylanica II no. 17 (pp. 98–123), from the Zenodo OCR of the volume, and cross-read against the SIDDHAM transcription and translation IN03081 (Zenodo 3581077), which reproduces the same edition; the North Gate slab (no. 28) and Wickremasinghe's remarks on the king's claims (no. 29, p. 167) were read in the same volume. Armour (1834) and Müller (1883) were not read; they are known here only through Wickremasinghe's account of them, including Müller's argument about Sagiri. Bell's A.S.C. Annual Report of 1903 was not read directly; his measurements and phrases come from Wickremasinghe's quotations. The Culavamsa's account of Nissanka Malla could not be reached in a legible text and nothing is claimed from it; the Pujavaliya and Rajavaliya were not reached, which is why the 'sixty hours' claim is held as unverified. District: a Nominatim reverse geocode at zoom 10 of the slab's position returns Polonnaruwa District (LK-72), and the UNESCO listing places the ancient city in the same district. Coordinates are approximate, from the geotags of Commons photographs taken beside the slab (7.9477, 81.0017) and of the Vatadage (OSM way 275333336 at 7.9473, 81.0015); Overpass could not be reached to find a node for the slab itself. District budget: Polonnaruwa stood at 3 on the slate without GRP-02 and GRP-03 (IDEA-0007, IDEA-0122, IDEA-0155), no GRP-02 film is proposed there, and this film takes it to 4; the reopened GRP-03 slots may still move it. Differentiation: no other film on the slate is wholly built on an inscription (the GRP-03 katikavata film that once held that archetype was replaced), and none in either group is set inside this terrace; but see the audit note below on IDEA-0025. Against the group's films currently written: a wind-and-surf shore (0035), a sinkhole descent (0039) and a white-noon telephoto city (0042); this is the only one whose single move is a level traverse at page height in first raking sun. The other GRP-03 slots were reopened on 2026-09-26 and are not compared here. Against GRP-02 and the slate's nearest neighbours: the proposal's top-down drone rising vertically was dropped because IDEA-0055, another site carrying a slab of the same king, pays off on a vertical aerial climb; GRP-02's museum film (IDEA-0014) uses kneeling-height dolly moves on an object indoors, and this film's traverse is outdoors, continuous and runs off its object into a landscape. Persons named in the voice are Nissanka Malla and Wickremasinghe; neither is named in any other voice on the slate, in GRP-02's picks, or in the GRP-03 proposals. Bell and Paranavitana are kept out of the voice because they are in other films' voices. Images: four Commons files confirmed through the API (existence, licence and a viewed thumbnail); the Hatadage image is of the relic house beside the slab, not the slab. Fallback in a different district: none carries this story; the removal order survives only on this king's slabs in this city, and his inscription at Dambulla (Matale, closed) does not carry it. If the traverse or the raking light cannot be had, the recommendation is to drop the film rather than make it from a crowded midday site. Audit 2026-09-26: GRP-02's IDEA-0025, written the same day, opens and closes on an inscribed stone post and moves a lens across its carved lines; the two films collide on the inscription archetype and on the reading move, and connections and risks now say so.
